tests.title: Unit 6: Stock Markets and Mutual Funds – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: A company issues shares for the first time to the public through an offer document. This is called:
options: An Initial Public Offering
A Bonus Issue
A Rights Issue
A Follow-on Public Offer

questions.question_text: Existing shareholders of a company are offered new shares in proportion to their holdings, usually at a price lower than the market price. This is a:
options: Preference allotment
Bonus issue
Private placement
Rights issue

questions.question_text: When a company issues free additional shares to existing shareholders out of its reserves, it is a:
options: Qualified placement
Public issue
Rights issue
Bonus issue

questions.question_text: A company declares a 1:2 bonus. A shareholder holding 600 shares will receive:
options: 600 additional shares
300 additional shares
1,200 additional shares
200 additional shares

questions.question_text: After a 1:1 bonus issue, the market price per share, other things being equal, will tend to:
options: Double from the earlier price
Fall to about half of the earlier price
Remain exactly the same as before
Fall to zero immediately

questions.question_text: A stock split of one share of face value Rs 10 into two shares of Rs 5 each leads to:
options: A halving of the number of shares with a doubling of the price
A doubling of the number of shares with no change in the total market value
A fall in the market capitalisation of the company by half
No change in the number of shares but a fall in the face value

questions.question_text: The market where new securities are issued for the first time is the:
options: Primary market
Forward market
Money market
Secondary market

questions.question_text: The market where existing securities are bought and sold among investors is the:
options: Secondary market
Call money market
Treasury bill market
Primary market

questions.question_text: The two major stock exchanges in India are:
options: RBI and SEBI
NABARD and SIDBI
BSE and NSE
MCX and NCDEX

questions.question_text: The benchmark index of the BSE is the:
options: Bank Nifty
India VIX
Nifty 50
Sensex

questions.question_text: The benchmark index of the NSE is the:
options: Sensex
BSE 500
Nifty 50

questions.question_text: The Sensex consists of how many stocks?
The regulator of the Indian securities market is:
options: SEBI
PFRDA
IRDAI
RBI

questions.question_text: To trade in shares on the stock exchange, an investor requires:
options: A savings bank account alone, with a debit card attached
A demat account, a trading account and a bank account
A PAN card alone, along with a passport size photograph
An Aadhaar card alone, along with the proof of address

questions.question_text: A demat account is used to:
options: Hold the securities in the electronic form
Hold the cash in the electronic form
Hold the property papers in the physical form
Hold the gold in the physical form

questions.question_text: The depositories in India are:
options: NSDL and CDSL
BSE and NSE
LIC and GIC
SEBI and RBI

questions.question_text: A Depository Participant (DP) is:
options: An agent of the depository, like a bank or a broker, that opens demat accounts
A regulator who supervises the working of the depositories in India
A stock exchange that lists the debt securities of the companies
A company that issues new shares to the public through an IPO

questions.question_text: Settlement of trades in Indian equity markets is now done on a:
options: T+5 basis
T+10 basis
T+1 basis
Same day basis only for the cash
questions.explanation: Trade date plus one working day.

questions.question_text: Face value of a share is:
options: The nominal value printed on the share certificate
The book value as shown in the balance sheet
The price at which the company bought back the share
The price at which it trades in the market

questions.question_text: A share of face value Rs 10 trades at Rs 250 in the market. The premium over the face value is:
options: Rs 240
Rs 10
Rs 250
Rs 260

questions.question_text: The dividend declared as 40% on a share of face value Rs 10 means a dividend per share of:
options: Rs 25
Rs 0.4
Rs 40
Rs 4

questions.question_text: An investor owns 500 shares of face value Rs 10. The company declares a dividend of 150%. The dividend received is:
options: Rs 750

questions.question_text: Dividend yield = dividend per share / market price × 100. A share paying Rs 6 per share dividend and trading at Rs 200 has a yield of:
Earnings per share (EPS) = net profit after tax / number of shares. A company has a PAT of Rs 50 crore and 10 crore shares. EPS is:
options: Rs 50
Rs 0.5
Rs 500
Rs 5

questions.question_text: Price-earnings (P/E) ratio = market price / EPS. If the price is Rs 150 and EPS is Rs 10, the P/E ratio is:

tests.title: Unit 6: Stock Markets and Mutual Funds – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: A high P/E ratio generally indicates that investors:
options: Expect the company to go bankrupt very soon
Expect high growth in the future earnings of the company
Expect the dividends to be stopped completely
Expect the price of the share to fall to zero

questions.question_text: Book value per share = net worth / number of shares. A company with net worth Rs 400 crore and 20 crore shares has a book value per share of:
options: Rs 20
Rs 200
Rs 2

questions.question_text: Market capitalisation of a company is:
options: Total debt added to the total equity of the company
Net profit multiplied by the number of shares outstanding
Market price per share multiplied by the number of shares outstanding
Face value per share multiplied by the number of shares

questions.question_text: A company with 5 crore shares trades at Rs 400 per share. Its market capitalisation is:
options: Rs 200 crore
Rs 2,000 crore
Rs 405 crore
Rs 80 crore

questions.question_text: A "large-cap" company is generally one that:
options: Ranks beyond the 250th by market capitalisation
Has a face value above Rs 100 per share
Ranks among the top 100 companies by market capitalisation
Ranks between 101 and 250 by market capitalisation

questions.question_text: A bull market is one in which prices are:
options: Falling, with the investor pessimism
Constant, with no trading
Rising, with the investor optimism
Volatile with no trend

questions.question_text: A bear market is one in which prices are:
options: Rising, with the investor optimism
Falling, with the investor pessimism
Rising only in the debt market
Constant, with no trading

questions.question_text: A market order to buy a share is executed:
options: Only at the opening price of the next day
At the best available price at the time
Only at the price specified by the investor
Only at the closing price of the day

questions.question_text: A limit order to buy at Rs 100 will be executed:
options: Only at Rs 110
At Rs 100 or higher
At any price in the market
At Rs 100 or lower

questions.question_text: A stop-loss order is placed to:
options: Increase the profit by buying when the price rises
Limit the loss by selling when the price falls to a set level
Convert the shares into the cash at the end of the day
Cancel all the earlier orders of the investor

questions.question_text: Intraday trading means:
options: Buying only the debt securities issued by the government
Buying the shares only through an initial public offering
Holding the shares in the demat account for more than a year
Buying and selling the same security on the same trading day

questions.question_text: Delivery-based trading means:
options: Trading only in the futures
Trading only in the bonds
Taking the shares into the demat account after buying
Squaring off the position on the same day

questions.question_text: Short selling means:
options: Selling shares at a price which is higher than the market price
Selling shares only for a short period of time after buying them
Selling the shares of small companies only in the market
Selling shares one does not own, hoping to buy them back cheaper

questions.question_text: Circuit breakers in the stock market are used to:
options: Increase the trading volume during the crisis
Halt trading when prices rise or fall beyond the set limits
Allow trading after the market hours
Change the face value of shares

questions.question_text: The settlement guarantee on the stock exchange is provided by the:
options: Clearing corporation
Depository participant
Income tax department
Company issuing the shares

questions.question_text: Brokerage is:
options: The tax paid on the profit of the trade
The interest paid on the margin
The dividend paid to the shareholder
The fee charged by the broker for executing a trade

questions.question_text: Securities Transaction Tax (STT) is levied on:
options: The profit made on the sale of a residential house by an individual
The salary received by a broker from the stock exchange
The interest earned on the bank deposits by an individual
The purchase and sale of listed securities on the recognised exchanges

questions.question_text: Long-term capital gain on the sale of listed equity shares applies if they are held for:
options: More than 12 months
More than 24 months
More than 36 months
More than 6 months

questions.question_text: Short-term capital gain on listed equity shares applies when the holding period is:
options: More than 36 months
More than 24 months
More than 12 months
12 months or less

questions.question_text: Shares bought at Rs 100 and sold at Rs 160 after 8 months. The gain of Rs 60 per share is a:
options: Dividend income
Short-term capital gain
Business loss
Long-term capital gain

questions.question_text: A debenture is:
options: A policy of the insurance company
A certificate of the mutual fund unit
A share in the ownership of the company
A debt instrument issued by a company to raise a loan

questions.question_text: A bond differs from a share in that a bond holder:
options: Is an owner and receives the dividends, whereas a shareholder is a lender
Is a lender and receives fixed interest, whereas a shareholder is an owner
Has the voting rights in the company, whereas a shareholder does not
Shares the profits of the company, whereas a shareholder gets fixed interest

questions.question_text: A bond of face value Rs 1,000 pays 8% coupon. The annual interest is:
options: Rs 8
Rs 800
Rs 80

questions.question_text: If the market price of a bond rises, its yield:
options: Falls
Remains the same
Rises
Becomes zero

questions.question_text: When interest rates in the economy rise, the prices of the existing fixed-rate bonds generally:
options: Double
Fall
Remain the same
Rise

tests.title: Unit 6: Stock Markets and Mutual Funds – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: Government securities are:
options: Insurance policies issued by the Life Insurance Corporation
Equity shares issued by the government-owned companies to the public
Mutual fund units issued by the public sector banks to investors
Debt instruments issued by the government with a very low risk of default

questions.question_text: Treasury bills are short-term government securities with a maturity of:
options: Less than one year
Ten years
Twenty years
Five years

questions.question_text: Commercial paper is:
options: A mutual fund unit issued by the banks
A long-term secured debenture issued by the companies
An equity share issued by the companies
A short-term unsecured promissory note issued by companies

questions.question_text: The mutual fund is:
options: A pool of money from many investors, invested in securities by professionals
A stock exchange where the shares are bought and sold daily
A bank that accepts the deposits and gives the loans to the public
An insurance company that sells the life and general policies

questions.question_text: The mutual funds in India are regulated by:
options: IRDAI
RBI
SEBI
NABARD

questions.question_text: The Association of Mutual Funds in India is abbreviated as:
options: CDSL
AMFI
SEBI
NSDL

questions.question_text: The price of one unit of a mutual fund scheme is its:
options: Net Asset Value
Market capitalisation
Expense ratio
Face value

questions.question_text: NAV per unit = (total assets − total liabilities)/number of units. If assets are Rs 120 crore, liabilities Rs 20 crore and units 5 crore, NAV is:
options: Rs 24
Rs 20
Rs 100
Rs 4

questions.question_text: An investor invests Rs 50,000 in a fund at NAV Rs 25. The units received are:
options: 500 units
2,000 units
25,000 units

questions.question_text: If the NAV rises to Rs 30 for the 2,000 units, the value of the investment is:
An open-ended mutual fund scheme allows investors to:
options: Redeem units only at the end of the scheme
Buy units only during the new fund offer
Buy and redeem units at any time at the NAV
Sell the units only on the stock exchange

questions.question_text: A closed-ended scheme has:
options: A fixed maturity, with units bought only during the new fund offer
Units that can be redeemed every day at the NAV of that day
No exit load even for an early exit from the scheme
No maturity, with units available for purchase at any time

questions.question_text: An equity mutual fund invests mainly in:
options: Real estate
Shares of companies
Gold bars
Government bonds

questions.question_text: A debt mutual fund invests mainly in:
options: Commodities traded on the commodity exchanges
Bonds, debentures and money market instruments
Gold bars and the coins kept in the vaults of the banks
Shares of the listed companies on the stock exchanges

questions.question_text: A hybrid fund invests in:
options: Only gold
Only debt
A mix of equity and debt
Only equity

questions.question_text: An index fund aims to:
options: Invest in gold along with the index
Invest only in the debt of the index companies
Beat the market index by active stock picking
Replicate the performance of a market index such as Nifty 50

questions.question_text: An ETF (exchange-traded fund) differs from a regular open-ended fund in that an ETF:
options: Has no underlying securities
Cannot be bought through a demat account
Can be bought only from the fund house at NAV
Trades on the stock exchange like a share

questions.question_text: A liquid fund invests in:
options: Real estate projects with a long-term lock-in of the money
Gold exchange-traded funds with a long-term holding period
Very short-term debt and money market instruments of up to 91 days
Equity shares of the companies with a long-term growth outlook

questions.question_text: An ELSS is a mutual fund that:
options: Invests only in debt and carries a lock-in of 10 years
Invests in gold and carries no lock-in period at all
Invests in real estate and carries a lock-in of 5 years
Invests mainly in equity and gives a Section 80C deduction with a 3-year lock-in

questions.question_text: SIP stands for:
options: Share Indexed Portfolio
Systematic Investment Plan
Simple Interest Plan
Secured Investment Policy

questions.question_text: In a SIP, an investor:
options: Invests a large lump sum when the market is at its peak
Invests only when the market has fallen by a large margin
Invests only in the new fund offers of the fund houses
Invests a fixed amount at regular intervals, whatever the market level

questions.question_text: The benefit of rupee cost averaging in a SIP is that:
options: More units are bought when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high
The NAV of the scheme never falls during the period of the SIP
The same number of units is bought every month whatever the NAV
Only the units at the lowest NAV of the year are bought

questions.question_text: A SIP of Rs 5,000 per month buys units at NAVs of Rs 20, Rs 25 and Rs 40 in three consecutive months. The total number of units bought is:
options: 625 units
375 units
600 units
575 units

questions.question_text: A SIP of Rs 4,000 per month buys units at NAVs of Rs 20 and Rs 40 in two months. The total units are:
options: 400 units
200 units
300 units
100 units

questions.question_text: With the above, the average cost per unit is:
options: Rs 30
Rs 40
Rs 25

tests.title: Unit 6: Stock Markets and Mutual Funds – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: The expense ratio of a mutual fund is:
options: The dividend paid every year
The annual fee charged by the fund as a percentage of the assets
The fee paid by the investor to the broker on each trade
The tax paid on the gains

questions.question_text: Exit load is:
options: A tax levied by the government on the dividends received
A fee paid by the fund house to the investor on redemption
A fee charged when units are redeemed before a specified period
A fee charged when units are bought from the fund house

questions.question_text: A direct plan of a mutual fund compared with a regular plan has:
options: A lower expense ratio as there is no distributor commission
A higher expense ratio due to the distributor commission
No NAV
A lock-in period of 10 years

questions.question_text: In a growth option of a mutual fund:
options: Profits are paid out regularly to the investor
The NAV remains fixed forever
Profits are reinvested and reflected in the rising NAV
The units are redeemed automatically

questions.question_text: In the IDCW option of a mutual fund:
options: The NAV never falls even when a payout is made to investors
The units are doubled on every payout made to the investors
A part of the gains may be paid out and the NAV falls by the payout
No payout is ever made to the investors in the scheme

questions.question_text: The risk-o-meter for the mutual fund schemes shows:
options: The rate of return of the scheme every year
The expense ratio of the scheme
The level of risk of the scheme from low to very high
The name of the fund manager

questions.question_text: A person with a low risk appetite and a short horizon of one year should prefer:
options: A liquid or short-duration debt fund
A small-cap equity fund
A thematic equity fund
A sectoral equity fund

questions.question_text: A person saving for retirement 25 years away can consider a larger share of:
options: Savings accounts, since they carry no risk of loss at all
Cash kept at home, since it is the safest of all options
Gold coins only, since gold never falls in price in the long run
Equity funds, since equity tends to beat inflation over long periods

questions.question_text: Asset allocation means:
options: Dividing investments among asset classes like equity, debt and gold
Putting the entire money of the investor in a single good stock
Selling all the assets at the end of the financial year
Buying the assets with the help of a loan from a bank

questions.question_text: Diversification reduces:
options: The company-specific (unsystematic) risk of the portfolio
The taxes payable on the income from the portfolio
The rate of inflation in the economy of the country
The market-wide (systematic) risk of the portfolio completely

questions.question_text: Systematic risk is the risk that:
options: Can be removed by buying more shares of the same company
Exists only in the debt market
Affects the entire market and cannot be eliminated by diversification
Affects a single company only

questions.question_text: The beta of a stock measures:
options: The dividend paid by the stock to its shareholders every year
The brokerage payable on the trades in the stock
The sensitivity of the stock's returns to the returns of the market
The face value of the stock as printed on its certificate

questions.question_text: A stock with a beta of 1.5, when the market rises by 10%, is expected to rise by:
A stock with a beta of 0.5, when the market falls by 10%, is expected to fall by:
The return on an investment of Rs 10,000 that grows to Rs 12,500 in one year is:
Rs 10,000 grows to Rs 14,400 in 2 years at a compound rate. The annual compound rate is:
The rule of 72 says that money doubles in how many years at 12% annual compound return?
options: About 12 years
About 6 years
About 9 years
About 3 years

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be a sign of a possible stock market scam?
options: Information filed by the company with the exchange
Tips promising assured high returns from unregistered advisers
Investor education by SEBI
Quarterly results published by the company

questions.question_text: A pump-and-dump scheme involves:
options: Buying and holding a stock for the long term for the dividends
Investing in a mutual fund through a monthly SIP over many years
Applying for an IPO through the ASBA facility of a bank
Inflating a stock's price by false hype and then selling at the high price

questions.question_text: Insider trading is:
options: Trading by the investors in the demat form
Trading by the mutual funds with the fund managers' discretion
Dealing in securities on the basis of unpublished price sensitive information
Trading by the brokers on the exchange

questions.question_text: ASBA (Application Supported by Blocked Amount) in an IPO means that:
options: The application money stays in the investor's account and is blocked until the allotment
The application is made only on paper
The application money is paid in cash to the broker
The application money is paid to the company at the time of applying

questions.question_text: UPI-based IPO applications allow the investor to:
options: Pay the amount to the company by cheque
Block the application money through the UPI mandate
Pay the amount to the broker in cash
Apply without any money

questions.question_text: The SEBI platform for lodging the complaints against the listed companies and brokers is:
options: NACH
BHIM
SCORES
DigiLocker

questions.question_text: A recognised way to check whether an adviser is registered is:
options: The list of registered advisers and brokers on the SEBI website
The recommendation made by a friend who has invested with him
The advertisements of the adviser on the social media platforms
The number of followers the adviser has on a messaging platform

questions.question_text: A key principle for a first-time investor in the stock market is to:
options: Invest the entire savings in an IPO that is being talked about
Invest surplus money only, diversify and invest for the long term after learning
Borrow money to invest the entire amount in a single stock
Follow the tips given by unknown persons on the messaging apps
